Indexing, item assignment and len() use the same field order. For placement results, prefer values supplied by flPackage.getAccentsInfo rather than inventing an offset. text: A single Bézier segment.
title: fontlab.CurveEx

text: When you look at a letterform's outline in FontLab, you see a series of nodes connected by curve segments. Internally, each of those curve segments is stored as a CurveEx object. It holds four points — the two on-curve endpoints and the two off-curve control points (the "handles") — and provides mathematical operations on that single Bézier segment. Most designers won't use CurveEx directly unless they are writing geometry-processing scripts. The most common way to encounter CurveEx objects is through flShapeData.segments , which gives you all segments of a shape as a flat list for bulk processing.
title: What is CurveEx?

text: import fontlab as fl # ============================================================ # Get the segments from a shape. # flShapeData.segments gives you a flat list of all Bézier # segments for every contour in the shape. # ============================================================ font = fl . CurrentFont () glyph = font [ 'S' ] # 'S' has nice smooth curves to inspect layer = glyph . layers [ 0 ] shape = layer . shapes [ 0 ] segs = shape . shapeData . segments print ( f "Total Bézier segments in 'S': { len ( segs ) } " ) # ============================================================ # Print the basic geometry of each segment. # Each segment goes from p0 (start node) to p1 (end node), # with bcp0 and bcp1 as the off-curve control handles. # ============================================================ for i , seg in enumerate ( segs ): if not seg . empty (): length = seg . fastLength () kind = "line" if seg . countPoints == 1 else "curve" print ( f "Segment { i } ( { kind } ): " f "p0=( { seg . p0 . x () : .0f } , { seg . p0 . y () : .0f } ) → " f "p1=( { seg . p1 . x () : .0f } , { seg . p1 . y () : .0f } ) " f "length≈ { length : .0f } " ) # ============================================================ # Find all smooth joins in the glyph. # A smooth join is where two consecutive segments share a # node whose handles are collinear — no corner, just a smooth # transition. This is what you see as a "smooth node" in the UI. # ============================================================ smooth_count = 0 for i in range ( 1 , len ( segs )): if segs [ i ] . smooth ( segs [ i - 1 ]): smooth_count += 1 print ( f " \n Smooth joins: { smooth_count } out of { len ( segs ) - 1 } " ) # ============================================================ # Find potential missing extremum nodes. # An extremum is a topmost/bottommost/leftmost/rightmost point. # If a curve reaches its extreme inside a segment (not at a # node), that is a "missing extremum" — important for correct # PostScript hinting and clean vector export. # ============================================================ print ( " \n Potential missing extrema:" ) missing = 0 for i in range ( 1 , len ( segs )): if segs [ i ] . extremum ( segs [ i - 1 ]): missing += 1 print ( f " At node { i } : ( { segs [ i ] . p0 . x () : .0f } , { segs [ i ] . p0 . y () : .0f } )" ) if missing == 0 : print ( " None found — all extrema have nodes." )

text: Font export configuration.
title: fontlab.ExportControl

text: When you export a font (File → Export Font As), FontLab reads a set of parameters: which export profile (OpenType PS, Variable TTF, etc.), where to put the files, how to handle conflicts. ExportControl lets scripts access and modify these parameters programmatically. The most common use is in automation scripts that export many fonts to a predictable location: set the profile, set the folder, set conflictMode = 0 (overwrite), then call the export command. This is the scripting equivalent of clicking through the Export Font dialog.
title: What is ExportControl?

text: import fontlab as fl from fontlab import ExportControl # ============================================================ # Set up a clean export configuration for batch use. # This is the scripting equivalent of filling in the # Export Font As dialog and clicking OK. # ============================================================ ec = ExportControl () ec . init () # always start from clean defaults # Choose the export profile: ec . profileName = "OpenType PS" # OTF with CFF outlines # Tell FontLab where to put the exported files: ec . destinationMode = 1 # 1 = custom folder ec . destinationFolder = "/tmp/exported_fonts/" # absolute path # Don't ask about conflicts — just overwrite: ec . conflictMode = 0 # 0 = overwrite existing files # Export the full font (not just selected glyphs): ec . contentMode = 0 # 0 = full font # Organise output by family name (all styles in one folder): ec . groupFamily = True print ( f "Export config: ' { ec . profileName } ' → ' { ec . destinationFolder } '" ) # ============================================================ # Save settings so they persist for next time. # ============================================================ ec . store () print ( "Settings saved." ) # ============================================================ # Load previously saved settings and adjust one field. # Useful if you want to preserve most settings but change the # profile for this run. # ============================================================ ec2 = ExportControl () if ec2 . load (): print ( f "Loaded profile: ' { ec2 . profileName } '" ) ec2 . profileName = "Variable TTF" # override just the profile print ( f "Changed to: ' { ec2 . profileName } '" ) else : print ( "No saved settings found — starting from defaults." )

text: A single font audit finding.
title: fontlab.FaBasicPtr

text: When you run FontLab's font audit (the grid of checkmarks in Font Window → Font Audit), the engine inspects every glyph for common outline problems: open contours, reversed winding, nearly-straight curves that should be lines, extremum nodes that are missing, and so on. Each detected problem is an FaBasic record. In scripts, you access FaBasic records through flAuditInfo.basic . The most useful scripting workflow is: 1. Run the audit (open the Font Audit panel to populate results). 2. Iterate the findings via flAuditInfo objects. 3. For each auto-fixable finding ( canBeFixed == True ), call fix() . 4. Call fl.Update() to refresh the display. (Registered as FaBasicPtr in source; Python sees it as FaBasic )

Access them through the canvas info # system after running the audit. # # This example shows how to print and optionally auto-fix # all audit findings for a specific glyph. # ============================================================ font = fl . CurrentFont () glyph = font [ 'S' ] # try a glyph with complex curves # Run the audit for this glyph's first layer: layer = glyph . layers [ 0 ] # Access audit results (method name may vary by version): # audit_items = layer.auditResults() # returns list of flAuditInfo # For demonstration, we simulate what you would do with the results: # for audit_info in audit_items: # b = audit_info.basic # print(f"Issue: {b.title}") # print(f" Priority: {b.priority}") # print(f" Location: ({b.location.x():.0f}, {b.location.y():.0f})") # print(f" Report: {b.report}") # print(f" Can be fixed: {b.canBeFixed}") # # if b.canBeFixed: # result = b.fix() # if result: # print(f" → Auto-fixed! Glyph '{result.name}' updated.") # else: # print(f" → Fix returned Nothing.") # ============================================================ # After fixing any issues, always update the display: # ============================================================ fl . Update () print ( "Audit review complete." )

text: Vertical metric values for one master.
title: fontlab.FontMetrics

text: Every master in a font has a set of vertical metrics: how tall is the tallest letter, how far does the descender drop below the baseline, how tall are the lowercase letters, and so on. FontMetrics is a simple container that holds these six values for one master. These are the values that determine the overall proportions of your design: - UPM — the grid size. All other values are relative to this. - Ascender — the top of tall lowercase letters like 'd', 'h', 'l'. Typically 70–80% of UPM. - Descender — the bottom of descending letters like 'g', 'p', 'y'. Typically -20% to -30% of UPM (negative). - x-height — the top of short lowercase letters like 'x', 'n', 'o'. Typically 45–55% of UPM. - Cap height — the top of uppercase letters like 'H', 'I'. Typically 60–75% of UPM. - Line gap — extra space between lines. Usually 0 for most text fonts. You will use FontMetrics mainly to read or verify master-specific metrics in scripts. For the values exported into the OpenType tables, use FontInfo instead.
title: What is FontMetrics?

text:
import fontlab as fl from fontlab import FontMetrics font = fl . CurrentFont () # ============================================================ # Read the vertical metrics from the first master. # ============================================================ master = font . masters [ 0 ] fm = FontMetrics ( font , master ) print ( f "Metrics for master ' { master } ':" ) print ( f " UPM: { fm . upm : .0f } " ) print ( f " Ascender: { fm . ascender : .0f } " ) print ( f " Descender: { fm . descender : .0f } " ) print ( f " x-Height: { fm . xHeight : .0f } " ) print ( f " Cap Height: { fm . capsHeight : .0f } " ) print ( f " Line Gap: { fm . lineGap : .0f } " ) # ============================================================ # Compute some useful ratios from the metrics. # These ratios describe the proportions of the typeface. # ============================================================ total_height = fm . ascender - fm . descender x_ratio = fm . xHeight / fm . upm * 100 cap_ratio = fm . capsHeight / fm . upm * 100 print ( f " 
 Proportions:" ) print ( f " Total height (asc-dsc): { total_height : .0f } units" ) print ( f " x-height / UPM: { x_ratio : .1f } %" ) print ( f " Cap height / UPM: { cap_ratio : .1f } %" ) # ============================================================ # Check all masters have consistent x-height values. # Inconsistent x-heights across masters cause problems in # variable fonts. # ============================================================ print ( " 
 Checking x-height consistency across masters:" ) x_heights = {} for master_name in font . masters : fm = FontMetrics ( font , master_name ) x_heights [ master_name ] = fm . xHeight print ( f " [ { master_name } ] x-height = { fm . xHeight : .0f } " ) values = list ( x_heights . values ()) if len ( set ( values )) == 1 : print ( "✓ All masters have the same x-height." ) else : print ( f "⚠ x-heights differ across masters!" ) for name , val in x_heights . items (): print ( f " { name } : { val : .0f } " ) # ============================================================ # Create a FontMetrics struct and set values manually. # Useful when you want to compare or document intended values. # ============================================================ target = FontMetrics ( 1000.0 ) # 1000 UPM target . ascender = 730 target . descender = - 270 target . xHeight = 540 target . capsHeight = 710 target . lineGap = 0 print ( f " 
 Target metrics: " f "asc= { target . ascender } dsc= { target . descender } " f "xh= { target . xHeight } cap= { target . capsHeight } " )

text: A component reference inside a composite glyph.
title: fontlab.GlyphComponent

text: A composite glyph is a glyph whose shapes are built entirely from references to other glyphs, rather than containing its own outlines. For example, the "é" (e-acute) glyph in most fonts does not contain its own curves — instead, it contains two component references: one to the "e" base glyph and one to "acutecomb" (the combining acute accent). Each of those references is a GlyphComponent . It identifies the base glyph (by name or ID), specifies where to place it (through a transform matrix), and optionally says whether to use anchor-to-anchor alignment instead of a fixed transform. GlyphComponent is the data object describing the reference. On the canvas, each component appears as an flShape with isComponent == True , and shape.component gives you the GlyphComponent data.
title: What is GlyphComponent?

text:
from PythonQt.QtGui import QTransform import fontlab as fl from fontlab import GlyphComponent font = fl . CurrentFont () # ============================================================ # Find all composite glyphs in the font and list their # component references. A composite is a glyph that has no # direct contours but contains component shapes. # ============================================================ print ( "--- Composite Glyphs ---" ) composite_count = 0 for glyph in font . glyphs : layer = glyph . layers [ 0 ] components_in_glyph = [] for shape in layer . shapes : if shape . isComponent : comp = shape . component if comp : # Resolve the component's base glyph name: try : base_glyph = font . glyph ( comp . name_id ) base_name = base_glyph . name if base_glyph else f "id= { comp . name_id } " except Exception : base_name = f "id= { comp . name_id } " components_in_glyph . append ( f "' { base_name } ' " f "(anchors= { comp . use_anchors } " f "width_scale= { comp . width_scale : .2f } )" ) if components_in_glyph : composite_count += 1 print ( f " ' { glyph . name } ': { ' + ' . join ( components_in_glyph ) } " ) print ( f " 
 Total composite glyphs: { composite_count } " ) # ============================================================ # Inspect the transform of a specific component. # For composites that use transforms (not anchors), the # translation tells you where the component was placed. # ============================================================ if 'eacute' in [ g . name for g in font . glyphs ]: glyph = font [ 'eacute' ] layer = glyph . layers [ 0 ] for shape in layer . shapes : if shape . isComponent : comp = shape . component tx = comp . transform dx = tx . dx () # horizontal translation dy = tx . dy () # vertical translation print ( f " 
 'eacute' component transform: dx= { dx : .0f } dy= { dy : .0f } " ) print ( f " use_anchors: { comp . use_anchors } " ) # ============================================================ # Create a GlyphComponent manually. # This shows what fields you would set to build a composite # from scratch in a script. # ============================================================ # Component referencing "e" by name: comp_e = GlyphComponent ( "e" ) comp_e . use_anchors = False comp_e . transform = QTransform () # identity (no offset) # Component referencing "acutecomb" placed 300 units above baseline: comp_acute = GlyphComponent ( "acutecomb" ) comp_acute . use_anchors = True # let the anchor system position it comp_acute . transform = QTransform () . translate ( 0 , 300 ) print ( " 
 Manual component created:" ) print ( f " 'e' component: use_anchors= { comp_e . use_anchors } " ) print ( f " 'acutecomb' component: use_anchors= { comp_acute . use_anchors } " )

text: Font Info data Complete font metadata.
title: fontlab.Info

text: Info is the metadata wrapper for all the descriptive information about your font that gets embedded in the file: the family name, style name, designer's name, copyright notice, license, all the OpenType metric values, PostScript hinting parameters, and much more. It follows the UFO (Unified Font Object) specification for attribute names, which means the property names like openTypeNameDesigner , openTypeOS2WeightClass , and postscriptFontName correspond directly to documented UFO 3 attributes. If you know UFO, you already know this interface. Access Info through package.info on an flPackage wrapper: package = fl . flPackage ( fl . CurrentFont ()) info = package . info print ( info . familyName ) info . copyright = "© 2026 My Foundry" All properties read/write the font's metadata storage directly. There is no need to call a save method — changes take effect immediately in the in-memory font.
title: What is Info?

text: These are the most important fields for most type designers. Name Type Description Access familyName string The primary family name shown in application font menus (e.g. "Helvetica", "Times New Roman"). All styles in the family should share this name. read/write styleName string The style name within the family (e.g. "Regular", "Bold Italic", "Condensed Light"). read/write styleMapFamilyName string The "linked family" name used for bold/italic style mapping in older applications. Applications that only understand the 4-style model (Regular/Bold/Italic/BoldItalic) use this to group styles. read/write styleMapStyleName string The style position within the linked family group. Must be one of exactly four values: "regular" , "italic" , "bold" , or "bold italic" . read/write copyright string The full copyright statement embedded in the font file (e.g. "Copyright 2026 My Foundry. All rights reserved."). read/write trademark string The trademark statement, if any. read/write note string Arbitrary free-text note about the font. Not shown to end users; used for internal documentation. read/write unitsPerEm int/float Units per em — the scale of the design grid. read/write descender int/float The descender value for this font's default UPM-relative metrics. read/write ascender int/float The ascender value. read/write xHeight int/float The x-height value. read/write capHeight int/float The cap height value. read/write italicAngle int/float The italic angle in degrees, measured counter-clockwise from vertical. 0 for upright fonts; typically -12 to -15 for italic. read/write versionMajor int The major version number of the font (e.g. the 1 in version 1.012 ). read/write versionMinor int The minor version number. read/write year int Year of creation. Deprecated in UFO 3 in favour of openTypeHeadCreated , but still supported. read/write panose string Legacy PANOSE classification — 10 space-separated numbers. Most modern workflows ignore PANOSE, but it is required for some font delivery platforms. read/write

import fontlab as fl font = fl . CurrentFont () info = font . info # FontInfo object — direct read/write access # ============================================================ # 1. Read the most important identification fields. # ============================================================ print ( "--- Font Identification ---" ) print ( f "Family: { info . familyName } " ) print ( f "Style: { info . styleName } " ) print ( f "Designer: { info . openTypeNameDesigner } " ) print ( f "Copyright: { info . copyright } " ) print ( f "Version: { info . versionMajor } . { info . versionMinor : 03d } " ) print ( f "UPM: { info . unitsPerEm } " ) # ============================================================ # 2. Check the key vertical metrics. # ============================================================ print ( " 
 --- Vertical Metrics ---" ) print ( f "Ascender: { info . ascender } " ) print ( f "Descender: { info . descender } " ) print ( f "x-Height: { info . xHeight } " ) print ( f "Cap Height: { info . capHeight } " ) print ( f "Italic Angle: { info . italicAngle } °" ) # ============================================================ # 3. Check OS/2 classification fields. # These determine how the font appears in weight/width menus. # ============================================================ print ( " 
 --- OS/2 Classification ---" ) print ( f "Weight class: { info . openTypeOS2WeightClass } " f "(400=Regular, 700=Bold)" ) print ( f "Width class: { info . openTypeOS2WidthClass } " f "(5=Normal, 3=Condensed)" ) print ( f "Vendor ID: ' { info . openTypeOS2VendorID } '" ) # ============================================================ # 4. Update copyright and license fields. # This is one of the most common pre-export scripts. # ============================================================ info . copyright = "Copyright 2026 My Foundry. All rights reserved." info . openTypeNameDesigner = "Jane Smith" info . openTypeNameDesignerURL = "https://myfoundry.example.com" info . openTypeNameManufacturer = "My Foundry" info . openTypeNameManufacturerURL = "https://myfoundry.example.com" info . openTypeNameLicense = ( "This Font Software is licensed under the SIL Open Font License, " "Version 1.1. This license is available with a FAQ at: " "https://scripts.sil.org/OFL" ) info . openTypeNameLicenseURL = "https://scripts.sil.org/OFL" info . versionMajor = 1 info . versionMinor = 0 print ( " 
 Identification fields updated." ) # ============================================================ # 5. Read PostScript hinting metadata. # These are the font-level values (separate from per-master # flHintingParameters, which override these). # ============================================================ print ( " 
 --- PostScript Blues ---" ) print ( f "BlueValues: { info . postscriptBlueValues } " ) print ( f "OtherBlues: { info . postscriptOtherBlues } " ) print ( f "StemSnapH: { info . postscriptStemSnapH } " ) print ( f "StemSnapV: { info . postscriptStemSnapV } " ) # ============================================================ # 6. Set the PostScript font name (required for OTF export). # The PS name should have no spaces and no special characters. # ============================================================ family = ( info . familyName or "MyFont" ) . replace ( " " , "" ) style = ( info . styleName or "Regular" ) . replace ( " " , "" ) info . postscriptFontName = f " { family } - { style } " info . postscriptFullName = f " { info . familyName } { info . styleName } " print ( f " 
 PS name set to: ' { info . postscriptFontName } '" )

text: Property Type Access Meaning nametablePath str or None read/write Font-wide custom .nam path; assignment reloads the mapping. Empty/None selects the standard mapping. otherData dict read/write Snapshot of additional settings; assign a dictionary to patch selected entries. font.info.nametablePath reads or sets the font-wide .nam path shown in Font Info > Other. Assignment reloads the mapping immediately. Use "" or None to restore the standard mapping. Relative paths resolve from the font's folder; an unreadable file retains its configured path and uses standard mapping with a warning. font.info.otherData returns a dictionary snapshot of the current master's Other settings (including loop resolution and TrueType hinting controls), plus the font-wide nametablePath . Assign a dictionary to patch selected entries; mutating the returned snapshot alone does not update the font. text: A parametric range on a contour.
title: fontlab.Interval

text: Imagine "selecting" a portion of a contour — not a node, but a stretch of curve from 25% to 75% of the way along the path. An Interval stores exactly that: two parametric values t0 and t1 defining a sub-range of a Bézier contour. Intervals are used internally by the node selection system, by split-curve operations, and by any tool that needs to work with a portion of a contour rather than whole segments. You will mostly encounter them when writing custom canvas tools that deal with selecting or cutting parts of curves.
title: What is Interval?

text:
from fontlab import Interval # ============================================================ # Create an interval covering the middle third of a contour. # This represents parametric positions 33.3% to 66.7% along # the contour arc. # ============================================================ iv = Interval () iv . setT0T1 ( 0.333 , 0.667 ) print ( f "Interval: t0= { iv . t0 : .3f } t1= { iv . t1 : .3f } " ) print ( f "Length: { iv . d : .3f } " ) print ( f "Midpoint: { iv . middle () : .3f } " ) print ( f "Is empty: { iv . isEmpty () } " ) # ============================================================ # Map a relative position within the interval to an # absolute contour position. # "Where is the 1/4 point of this interval on the contour?" # ============================================================ # 0.25 = 1/4 of the way through [0.333, 0.667] quarter_abs = iv . toAbsolute ( 0.25 ) print ( f " 
 1/4 through interval → absolute t = { quarter_abs : .3f } " ) # Expected: 0.333 + 0.25 * (0.667 - 0.333) = ~0.417 # Map back: given absolute t=0.5, where is that in the interval? fraction = iv . toInterval ( 0.5 ) print ( f "Absolute t=0.5 → interval fraction = { fraction : .3f } " ) # Expected: (0.5 - 0.333) / (0.667 - 0.333) = ~0.5 # ============================================================ # Reverse the interval — same coverage, opposite direction. # Useful when you need to iterate a selection in reverse. # ============================================================ rev = iv . reversed () print ( f " 
 Reversed: t0= { rev . t0 : .3f } t1= { rev . t1 : .3f } " ) # ============================================================ # An empty interval — covers nothing. # This is what you get when a hit test lands exactly on a node. # ============================================================ empty_iv = Interval () empty_iv . setT0T1 ( 0.5 , 0.5 ) print ( f " 
 Empty interval: isEmpty= { empty_iv . isEmpty () } d= { empty_iv . d } " )
title: Tutorial

text: from fontlab import Interval iv = Interval () iv . setT0T1 ( 0.2 , 0.8 ) def contains ( interval , t ): return interval . t0 <= t <= interval . t1 print ( contains ( iv , 0.5 )) # True print ( contains ( iv , 0.1 )) # False
title: Check whether a parametric position falls within an interval

text: from fontlab import Interval iv = Interval () iv . setT0T1 ( 0.0 , 1.0 ) third = iv . d / 3.0 parts = [] for i in range ( 3 ): part = Interval () part . setT0T1 ( iv . t0 + i * third , iv . t0 + ( i + 1 ) * third ) parts . append ( part ) print ( f "Part { i } : [ { part . t0 : .3f } , { part . t1 : .3f } ]" ) Constructors: Native bases: object Supplemental documentation: A numeric interval with t0 and t1 (both double) and d and key attributes. The captured declaration exposes isEmpty , middle , reversed , setT0T1 , toAbsolute and toInterval . Consult the retained constructor documentation for the supported creation forms.
